The verb typhlou ("to blind, to make blind") recalls Isaiah 6:10 (LXX), where God tells Isaiah to "make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes (kammyson tous ophthalmous auton), lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their hearts and turn and be healed." The blindness operates within a context of refusal — the people who cannot see are those who have not turned to the Lord (3:16).

The purpose of the blinding is specified: "to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God" (eis to me augasai ton photismon tou euangeliou tes doxes tou Christou, hos estin eikon tou theou). The sentence contains a cascade of genitives that must be parsed carefully. The "light" (photismos, "illumination, radiance, shining forth") belongs to "the gospel"; the gospel is "of the glory"; the glory belongs to "Christ"; and Christ is "the image of God" (eikon tou theou).

The word eikon ("image, likeness, representation") carries profound resonance. In Genesis 1:26-27 (LXX), God created humanity kat' eikona hemetran ("according to our image"). The eikon is not a copy but a visible manifestation of what is otherwise invisible — it makes the unseen visible. In Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, wisdom is described as "a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image (eikon) of his goodness." Paul calls Christ the eikon of God — the one who makes the invisible God visible. This language will be developed more fully in Colossians 1:15 ("He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation"), but here it serves the immediate argument: the glory that Moses' face reflected temporarily and fading (3:7, 13) is the same glory that shines permanently in Christ, who is the very image of God. The veil that prevents unbelievers from seeing the gospel is a veil that blocks them from seeing God's own glory displayed in Christ.

div.title: Verses 5-6: What Is Proclaimed and What Has Shone
div.p: "For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus' sake" (4:5).

The verse draws a sharp line between the messenger and the message. Paul does not proclaim himself (ou gar heautous keryssomen). The verb kerysso ("to proclaim, to herald, to announce publicly") is the word for the public announcement of a herald — the authoritative declaration of a king's message by the king's envoy. The herald does not announce himself; he announces his sovereign. Paul proclaims "Christ Jesus as Lord" (Christon Iesoun kyrion) — the formula places Christos and Iesous together and then adds kyrion as the predicate: the content of the proclamation is that the crucified Jesus is the Messiah and that the Messiah is Lord (kyrios). The title kyrios is the LXX's rendering of the divine name YHWH in hundreds of occurrences, and its application to Jesus throughout Paul's letters carries the full weight of that identification. The proclamation is that Israel's crucified Messiah has been given the name above every name — the name at which every knee bows (Philippians 2:9-11, drawing on Isaiah 45:23 LXX).

Paul and his co-workers, by contrast, are "your servants for Jesus' sake" (heautous de doulous hymon dia Iesoun — literally "ourselves as your slaves because of Jesus"). The word doulos ("slave, bondservant") is the strongest term for servitude in Greek. Paul identifies himself as the Corinthians' slave, and the reason is not the Corinthians' inherent authority over him but "because of Jesus" (dia Iesoun) — it is Jesus' lordship that makes Paul a slave to the community he serves. The reversal is total: the apostle who carries the surpassing glory of the new covenant (chapter 3) is simultaneously the slave of those to whom he proclaims it. This is the paradox that governs the entire chapter: the glory is God's; the vessel is a slave.
"For God, who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness,' has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (4:6).
This verse is the theological climax of the passage. Paul identifies a specific divine act — God shining light into hearts — and grounds it in the creation narrative.

"God, who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness'" (ho theos ho eipon ek skotous phos lampsei) — the reference is to Genesis 1:3 (LXX): kai eipen ho theos, genetheto phos, kai egeneto phos ("And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light"). God created light by speaking it into existence from within darkness. The darkness was the pre-creation chaos of Genesis 1:2 — tohu wabohu, "formless and void," with darkness over the face of the deep. God's first creative act was to speak light into that darkness.

Paul now says that the same God who performed that act of creation has performed a parallel act of illumination: "he has shone in our hearts" (hos elampsen en tais kardiais hemon). The verb lampein ("to shine, to give light, to radiate") describes the same kind of divine action as the creation of light — an act of sovereign power that brings illumination where there was none. The location of this shining is "in our hearts" (en tais kardiais hemon) — the seat of understanding, will, and perception in Jewish anthropology (cf. Deuteronomy 6:5, "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart"; Jeremiah 31:33 LXX 38:33, "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts").

The purpose of this illumination is stated with another cascade of genitives: "to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (pros photismon tes gnoseos tes doxes tou theou en prosopo Christou). The "light" (photismos) is "of the knowledge" (tes gnoseos); the knowledge is "of the glory" (tes doxes); the glory belongs to God (tou theou); and this glory is located "in the face of Jesus Christ" (en prosopo Christou).

The phrase "in the face of Jesus Christ" (en prosopo Christou) is the key that unlocks the entire preceding argument. In chapter 3, Paul discussed Moses' face (prosopon, 3:7, 13) — the face that shone with reflected glory, the face that had to be veiled because the glory was temporary and fading. Now Paul declares that the glory of God is displayed "in the face of Jesus Christ" — not reflected and fading, but direct and permanent. Moses' face radiated a borrowed glory that was being brought to an end (3:7, to katargoumenon); Christ's face radiates the glory of God himself (because Christ is the eikon of God, 4:4). The unveiled face of 3:18 — "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord" — finds its object here: what believers behold with unveiled face is the glory of God in the face of Christ.

The creation parallel is not decorative. Paul is arguing that the conversion of unbelievers is an act of new creation parallel to the original creation. Just as God spoke light into primordial darkness, God shines the knowledge of his glory into darkened hearts. The blinding performed by "the god of this age" (4:4) is a darkness that only the Creator can penetrate, just as the original darkness of Genesis 1:2 could only be dispelled by the Creator's word. The God who brings light from darkness is the same God in both acts, and the act of illumination is just as sovereign and just as creative. This places the gospel proclamation within a creation framework: those who receive the gospel have experienced a creative act of God as fundamental as the first creation.

div.title: Verse 7: The Thesis — Treasure in Clay Vessels
div.p: "But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (4:7).

The adversative de ("but") signals a contrast. The treasure (thesauros) is the glory just described — the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ, the content of the new covenant ministry. This treasure is contained in "jars of clay" (en ostrakinois skeuesin). The word ostrakinos ("made of baked clay, earthenware") describes the cheapest, most fragile, most common vessel available. Clay pots were everyday containers — used for storage, cooking, transport — and were easily broken. They had no intrinsic value. When broken, they were discarded.

The metaphor has precedent in Israel's scriptures. In Jeremiah 18:1-6, the LORD sends Jeremiah to the potter's house, where the potter works the clay on the wheel. When a vessel is spoiled, the potter reworks it as he sees fit. The LORD then says: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? Behold, like the clay (pelos) in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel" (Jeremiah 18:6 LXX). In Jeremiah 19:1-11, Jeremiah is told to buy a potter's earthen flask and then to smash it before the elders and priests as a sign of Jerusalem's coming destruction — "So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel (skeuos kerameos), so that it can never be mended" (19:11). In Isaiah 64:8 (LXX 64:7), Israel addresses God: "But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay (pelos), and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand." In Lamentations 4:2: "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold — how they are regarded as earthen pots (eis angeia ostrakina), the work of a potter's hands!"

The purpose clause is critical: "to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (hina he hyperbole tes dynameos e tou theou kai me ex hemon — literally "so that the surpassingness of the power may be of God and not from us"). The word hyperbole ("excess, surpassing quality, extraordinary measure") appeared in 1:8, where Paul's affliction in Asia was "beyond measure" (kath' hyperbolen). Here the same word describes the power — it is surpassing, extraordinary, beyond measure. And the purpose of placing this surpassing power in fragile clay vessels is to make its source unmistakable. If the apostle were impressive, powerful, eloquent, and visibly glorious, observers might attribute the ministry's effectiveness to the vessel. But when the vessel is visibly fragile, cracked, afflicted, and near death, the power that sustains the ministry can only be God's.

This is the same logic Paul deployed in 1 Corinthians 1:26-29: "For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God." The principle is identical: God deliberately selects inadequate vessels so that the power is unmistakably his. The clay vessel is not an accident or a failure; it is the design. The apostle's weakness is not a liability to be overcome but the intended means by which divine power is displayed.

div.title: Verses 8-9: The Catalogue of Afflictions — Pressed but Not Crushed
div.p: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed" (4:8-9).

These verses illustrate the clay-vessel thesis with four paired contrasts. Each pair names an affliction and then denies its final consequence. The structure is consistent: a present participle or adjective describes the condition, followed by a negative (ou/ouk) and a stronger term that describes what the affliction does not achieve.

First: "Afflicted in every way, but not crushed" (en panti thlibomenoi all' ou stenochroumenoi). The verb thlibo ("to press, to squeeze, to afflict") is the verbal form of thlipsis, the word that dominated the opening of the letter (1:4, 6, 8). The noun stenochoria ("narrowness, confinement, being hemmed in with no way out") appeared in Romans 2:9 alongside thlipsis and in Romans 8:35 in the catalogue of things that cannot separate from the love of Christ. To be thlibomenoi is to be under pressure from every direction; to be stenochroumenoi would be to be completely hemmed in with no escape. Paul is pressed, but not trapped.

Second: "Perplexed, but not driven to despair" (aporoumenoi all' ouk exaporoumenoi). The verb aporeo ("to be at a loss, to be without resources, to be perplexed") and its intensified form exaporeomai ("to be utterly at a loss, to despair completely") create a wordplay through intensification. The prefix ex- pushes the condition past the limit. Paul is aporeo — at a loss, without an obvious path forward. But he is not ex-aporeo — not driven past all recovery into total despair. This is significant because in 1:8, Paul used exaporethenai to describe his experience during the Asian affliction: "we despaired of life itself." There, Paul did reach the point of exaporeomai. But even in that extremity, he was sustained — delivered by "the God who raises the dead" (1:9). The present tense here in 4:8 describes the general apostolic experience: perplexity is constant, but it does not reach the point of final despair, because the God who raises the dead sustains through it.

Third: "Persecuted, but not forsaken" (diokomenoi all' ouk enkatalipomenoi). The verb dioko ("to pursue, to persecute, to chase") describes active hostile pursuit. The verb enkatalipo ("to abandon, to forsake, to leave behind") is the word used in the LXX for God's abandonment of his people — or, more precisely, for the fear that God has abandoned them. Psalm 22:1 (LXX 21:2): "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (hina ti enkatelipes me). Psalm 37:25 (LXX 36:25): "I have not seen the righteous forsaken (enkataleleimmenon)." Deuteronomy 31:6: "He will not leave you or forsake you" (ou me se ane kai ou me se enkatalipe). Paul is pursued by enemies, but God has not abandoned him. The persecutor presses, but the God who promised never to forsake his people has not broken that promise.

Fourth: "Struck down, but not destroyed" (kataballomenoi all' ouk apollymenoi). The verb kataballo ("to throw down, to knock down, to cast to the ground") describes being physically felled — knocked to the ground in combat. The verb apollymi ("to destroy, to ruin, to lose, to perish") is the same root as apollymenoi ("those who are perishing") in 4:3. Paul is knocked down but does not perish. The word links back to the veiled-gospel passage: those who are perishing (apollymenoi, 4:3) are those blinded by the god of this age. Paul, though struck down, does not join them. He is kataballomenos but not apollymenos — felled but not finished.

The four pairs create a cumulative picture of an apostle who lives continuously at the edge of destruction but is consistently held back from the final step. The power that holds him back is not his own resilience; it is the divine power identified in verse 7 as the reason for the clay vessel. The vessel cracks but does not shatter because the treasure within it sustains it.

div.title: Verses 10-12: Carrying the Death of Jesus — The Logic of the Cross in the Apostle's Body
div.p: "Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies" (4:10).

The word pantote ("always, at all times") indicates a permanent condition, not an occasional experience. The "death of Jesus" (ten nekrosin tou Iesou) uses the word nekrosis, which means "dying, deadness, the state of death, the process of being put to death." It is not thanatos ("death" as an event or power) but nekrosis — the ongoing experience of dying. Paul carries this dying of Jesus "in the body" (en to somati). The language is physical, not metaphorical. The afflictions catalogued in verses 8-9 are bodily experiences — pressure, perplexity, persecution, being struck down. Paul's body is the location where Jesus' dying is made visible.

The purpose clause (hina kai he zoe tou Iesou en tois somasin hemon phanerothe, "so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies") reveals the logic: the dying makes the living visible. The noun zoe ("life") stands in direct contrast to nekrosis ("dying"). Both are "of Jesus" (tou Iesou) — both belong to Jesus, both are aspects of Jesus' own experience. Jesus died and was raised; Paul carries the dying in his body so that the life of the risen Jesus becomes visible in the same body. The verb phaneroo ("to manifest, to make visible, to reveal, to display") connects to the phanerosis ("manifestation") of truth in verse 2. The apostle's body is a site of revelation: it displays the pattern of Jesus' own death and resurrection.

This is not abstract theology. It is a direct argument against Paul's critics. The rival teachers in Corinth apparently presented themselves with visible power, impressive credentials, and rhetorical skill (cf. 10:10, 11:5-6, 11:12-15). Paul's beaten, afflicted, fragile body was cited as evidence against his authority. Paul inverts the criticism: his broken body is not evidence of failure but the very means by which Jesus' life is displayed. The weakness authenticates the ministry because it makes the divine power unmistakable.
"For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh" (4:11).

The verse restates verse 10 with additional specificity. "We who live" (hemeis hoi zontes) — Paul and his co-workers are alive, and yet they are "always being given over to death" (aei eis thanaton paradidometha). The verb paradidomi ("to hand over, to deliver up, to give over") is the word used for Jesus' being "handed over" to death — the same verb used for Judas' betrayal (paradidomi in Matthew 26:15, Mark 14:10, Luke 22:4) and for God's act of handing over his Son (Romans 8:32, "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up [paredoken] for us all"). Paul is being paradidomi — handed over to death — in a way that mirrors Jesus' own being handed over. The passive voice (paradidometha) leaves the agent unspecified, but the pattern of the chapter suggests that God is the ultimate agent: the clay vessel is placed in harm's way so that the treasure within it can be displayed.

"For Jesus' sake" (dia Iesoun) — the suffering is not random; it is incurred because of Paul's identification with and service to Jesus. The phrase matches "for Jesus' sake" in verse 5, where Paul identified himself as the Corinthians' slave "because of Jesus."

"In our mortal flesh" (en te thnete sarki hemon) — the word thnetos ("mortal, subject to death") and sarx ("flesh") specify the location: not in some spiritual realm but in the physical, death-bound flesh of the apostle. The life of Jesus is manifested precisely where mortality is most evident.
"So death is at work in us, but life in you" (4:12).

This terse verse draws the conclusion. Death (ho thanatos) operates "in us" (en hemin) — in Paul and his apostolic team. Life (he zoe) operates "in you" (en hymin) — in the Corinthians. The apostle's dying produces life for the community. The logic is sacrificial: Paul's suffering, his exposure to death, his broken body — all of this serves the spiritual life of the Corinthians. The pattern is explicitly that of Jesus himself, whose death produced life for others. Paul does not claim to perform an atoning sacrifice; he claims to participate in the pattern of Jesus' self-giving death that generates life in others. The apostle's bodily suffering is the means by which the power of the gospel is transmitted to the community.

This verse also functions as a rebuke, though a gentle one. If death is at work in Paul and life in the Corinthians, then the Corinthians' vitality is purchased by Paul's suffering. Those in Corinth who despise Paul's weakness are despising the very means by which they received life.

div.title: Verses 13-15: The Spirit of Faith, Resurrection, and the Community's Benefit
div.p: "Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, 'I believed, and so I spoke,' we also believe, and so we also speak" (4:13).

Paul introduces a scriptural quotation to ground his response to suffering. "The same spirit of faith" (to auto pneuma tes pisteos) — "the same" (to auto) indicates continuity with someone or something. The question is: the same as whom? The answer comes from the quotation: Psalm 116:10 (LXX 115:1), episteuesa dio elalesa ("I believed, and so I spoke"). The psalmist is one who was afflicted to the point of death — "the snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish" (Psalm 116:3, LXX 114:3). In the midst of that extremity, the psalmist believed and therefore spoke. Paul claims "the same spirit of faith" as that psalmist — the faith that speaks even in the midst of affliction, the faith that does not fall silent under pressure but continues to proclaim.

The word pneuma here likely means "spirit" in the sense of disposition, attitude, or animating principle — "the same spirit of faith" that animated the psalmist animates Paul. Some interpreters may hear a reference to the Holy Spirit, and the two are not mutually exclusive: the disposition of faith is produced by the Spirit of God. But Paul's immediate point is the continuity between his own posture under suffering and the psalmist's: both believed, and therefore both spoke. Paul continues to proclaim the gospel despite affliction because his faith, like the psalmist's, compels speech.
"Knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence" (4:14).

The content of the faith that drives Paul's speech is now stated: it is resurrection faith. "He who raised the Lord Jesus" (ho egeiras ton kyrion Iesoun) identifies God as the agent of Jesus' resurrection — the same God identified in 1:9 as "the God who raises the dead." The verb egeiro ("to raise, to wake, to rouse") is the standard Pauline word for resurrection. God's raising of Jesus is the ground and guarantee that God "will raise us also" (kai hemas ... egerei). The future tense egerei expresses confidence: what God did for Jesus, God will do for Paul and his companions.

"With Jesus" (syn Iesou) — the preposition syn ("with, together with") indicates that the resurrection Paul anticipates is participation in Jesus' own resurrection. Paul will be raised together with Jesus, sharing in the same resurrection life. This is not a separate event modeled on Jesus' resurrection but a participation in it.

"And bring us with you into his presence" (kai parastesei syn hymin) — the verb paristemi ("to present, to place beside, to bring before") describes being brought before someone. The Corinthians are included: syn hymin ("with you"). Paul's hope is not individual survival but communal presentation before God. Apostle and community will be presented together. This directly connects to 1:14, where Paul anticipated mutual boasting "on the day of our Lord Jesus." The eschatological reunion is a shared event: Paul with the Corinthians, together before God. The verse also serves as reassurance: despite the death at work in Paul (4:12), the God who raises the dead will raise him and present him together with the Corinthians in God's presence.
"For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God" (4:15).

"It is all for your sake" (ta gar panta di' hymas) — everything Paul has described — the ministry, the affliction, the dying, the perseverance — is for the Corinthians' sake. The di' hymas ("because of you, for your sake") echoes 4:5 (doulous hymon dia Iesoun, "your slaves because of Jesus"). Paul's suffering is not self-referential; it has the Corinthians as its purpose.

The purpose extends beyond the Corinthians to a widening circle: "as grace extends to more and more people" (hina he charis pleonasasa dia ton pleionon ten eucharistian perisseuse). The verb pleonazo ("to increase, to multiply, to abound") describes grace (charis) expanding its reach through "the greater number" (ton pleionon, "the more, the majority, the increasing number"). As more people are reached by the gospel, the result is that "thanksgiving" (eucharistia) overflows (perisseuo). The ultimate purpose is "the glory of God" (eis ten doxan tou theou). The chain is complete: God's power sustains Paul through affliction; Paul's affliction-sustained ministry extends grace to more people; more people produce more thanksgiving; the thanksgiving serves God's glory. Every link in the chain is driven by grace and terminates in divine glory.

div.title: Verses 16-18: The Inner Renewal and the Weight of Glory
div.p: "So we do not lose heart" (4:16a).

The inclusio with verse 1 is completed: ouk enkakounen ("we do not lose heart"). The statement is now grounded in everything that has come between: the transparency of the ministry (4:2), the divine illumination that parallels creation (4:6), the clay-vessel design that displays God's power (4:7), the paradox of dying and living (4:10-12), and the resurrection hope (4:14). Paul has earned the right to repeat the declaration because he has shown why it is not bravado but theological conviction.
"Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (4:16b).

The contrast between "the outer person" (ho exo hemon anthropos) and "the inner person" (ho eso hemon) is not a Platonic dualism between body and soul. Paul is not denigrating the body in favor of an immaterial spirit. The "outer person" is the bodily, visible, public self that experiences the afflictions of verses 8-9 and carries the dying of Jesus (4:10). The "inner person" is the seat of renewal — the self that is being illuminated by God's creative light (4:6), the heart in which the Spirit has been given as a guarantee (1:22), the self that is being transformed "from one degree of glory to another" (3:18).

The verb diaphtheiro ("to waste away, to decay, to deteriorate, to corrupt") in the present passive (diaphtheiretai) describes an ongoing process. Paul's outer person is visibly deteriorating — the beatings, the hardships, the toll of years of apostolic labor are wasting him away. But the verb anakainoo ("to renew, to make new again") in the present passive (anakainoutai) describes a simultaneous, ongoing renewal. "Day by day" (hemera kai hemera) emphasizes the daily character of this renewal. Each day, as the outer person decays further, the inner person is renewed afresh.

The language connects to Psalm 103:5 (LXX 102:5): "who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed (anakainisthesetai) like the eagle's." The renewal is God's act: Paul does not renew himself. The one who renews the inner person is the same God who shines light into hearts (4:6) and who establishes, anoints, seals, and gives the Spirit (1:21-22). The two processes — wasting and renewal — operate simultaneously. The outward deterioration is real, not an illusion; and the inward renewal is equally real, not wishful thinking. The apostle lives in both realities at once.
"For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison" (4:17).

The verse operates by deliberate disproportion. Paul calls his affliction "light" (elaphron) and "momentary" (parautika). The word elaphros ("light, slight, trivial") is the same root as elaphria ("lightness, fickleness") in 1:17, where it described the charge of unreliability. The word parautika ("momentary, for the present moment, brief") confines the affliction to the present instant. These are startling descriptions given what Paul has endured: the near-death experience of 1:8-10, the constant persecution, the catalogue of sufferings that will be expanded in 6:4-10 and 11:23-33. Paul is not minimizing his suffering; he is measuring it against what it produces.

What the affliction produces is described with language that overwhelms the terms used for the suffering: "an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison" (aionion baros doxes kath' hyperbolen eis hyperbolen). The phrase piles weight upon weight:
"Eternal" (aionion) stands against "momentary" (parautika). The affliction occupies a moment; the glory occupies eternity.

"Weight" (baros, "heaviness, weightiness, burden, gravity") stands against "light" (elaphron). The affliction is light; the glory is heavy. In Hebrew, the word for "glory" (kavod) comes from the root k-v-d, meaning "heavy, weighty." The connection between glory and weight is embedded in the Hebrew language: glory is that which has weight, substance, gravity, significance. Paul may be exploiting this etymological connection. The glory has baros — weight, substance, permanence — in contrast to the lightness of present suffering.

"Beyond all comparison" (kath' hyperbolen eis hyperbolen) is a doubled intensifier that defies translation. The word hyperbole appears for the third time in this letter (after 1:8 and 4:7), and here it is doubled: the glory is hyperbole upon hyperbole, excess beyond excess, surpassing beyond surpassing. No comparison can capture the disproportion between present affliction and future glory.

The verb katergazomai ("to produce, to prepare, to accomplish, to work out") identifies the affliction as the active agent that produces the glory. The affliction does not merely precede the glory chronologically; it works the glory. The present suffering is preparatory — it is the process by which the eternal weight of glory is being worked out. This is not a theology of suffering as punishment or accident; it is a theology of suffering as preparation.
"As we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal" (4:18).

The participle skopounton hemon ("while we look at, while we fix our gaze on") describes the posture that sustains Paul through the disproportion of present affliction and future glory. The verb skopeo ("to look at, to observe, to fix attention on, to aim at") describes deliberate, focused attention — not a casual glance but a disciplined gaze. Paul's gaze is fixed not on "the things that are seen" (ta blepomena) but on "the things that are unseen" (ta me blepomena).

The final contrast defines the terms: "the things that are seen are transient" (ta gar blepomena proskaira) — the word proskairos ("transient, temporary, lasting only for a time, seasonal") describes what belongs to the present season, what has an expiration. "The things that are unseen are eternal" (ta de me blepomena aionia) — aionia, the same word used for the eternal weight of glory in verse 17. The visible world — including Paul's afflicted body, the persecution, the beatings, the near-death experiences — is proskaira, temporary, passing. The invisible reality — including the glory of God in the face of Christ, the inner renewal, the resurrection life, the weight of glory being prepared — is aionia, eternal, permanent.

This is not Platonic idealism, where the material world is dismissed as illusion. Paul does not call the visible world unreal — he calls it transient. The afflictions are real; they are also temporary. The unseen realities are both real and permanent. The apostle's capacity to endure present suffering without losing heart depends on this disciplined focus: eyes fixed on the eternal, not mesmerized by the temporary.

The verse sets up chapter 5 directly. If the seen is temporary and the unseen is eternal, then the mortal body (the "tent" of 5:1) is temporary, and the eternal dwelling God has prepared is permanent. If the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed, then the destruction of the earthly tent is not catastrophe but transition. The argument flows without interruption into 5:1: "For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."

div.title: The Chapter's Argument as a Whole
div.p: 2 Corinthians 4 is the central argument of a three-chapter unit (3-5) defending Paul's apostolic ministry. Chapter 3 established the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry and the unveiled access believers have to the glory of the Lord. Chapter 5 will address the eschatological destiny of the mortal body and the confidence that sustains Paul as he faces death. Chapter 4 sits between them, addressing the question that the juxtaposition of glory and affliction inevitably raises: if the ministry is so glorious, why is the minister so broken?
The answer unfolds in three movements.

First (4:1-6): the ministry is exercised with complete transparency — no cunning, no tampering, no hidden agendas. Where the gospel remains veiled, the blindness belongs to those being acted upon by the god of this age, not to any defect in the message. The content of the proclamation is not Paul but Christ Jesus as Lord, and the illumination that opens eyes to the gospel is an act of divine creation — the same God who spoke light into primordial darkness now shines in human hearts. Paul anchors the gospel in the Genesis creation narrative, making the reception of the gospel a new-creation event.

Second (4:7-12): the fragility of the apostle is by design. The treasure is in clay vessels so that the power is unmistakably God's. The affliction catalogue (4:8-9) demonstrates that Paul lives at the edge of destruction but is consistently held back from the final step. The reason is the death-and-life logic of the cross: Paul carries the dying of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus is displayed in the same body. Death is at work in the apostle, but life flows to the community. The apostle's weakness is not a liability but the mechanism of power's transmission.

Third (4:13-18): the faith that sustains this ministry is resurrection faith. Grounded in the same spirit of faith as the psalmist who believed and spoke even in affliction (Psalm 116:10), Paul proclaims because he knows that the God who raised Jesus will raise him also and present him together with the Corinthians. The chapter closes by reframing affliction as temporary and glory as eternal: the outer person wastes away while the inner person is renewed; the light momentary affliction prepares an eternal weight of glory; the visible is transient while the invisible is permanent. This disciplined focus on the unseen and eternal is what enables Paul to repeat, at the chapter's end, the declaration with which he began: "we do not lose heart."
Several threads connect this chapter to the rest of the letter and to 1 Corinthians.

The paradox of power in weakness, introduced in 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5 (the word of the cross as the power of God, the foolishness of preaching, Paul's own weakness and fear and trembling), reaches its fullest expression here. In 1 Corinthians, the paradox was stated as a principle; in 2 Corinthians 4, it is embodied in Paul's own battered body. The clay vessel is the physical instantiation of the theology of the cross.

The creation language of 4:6 (God speaking light into darkness) echoes the cosmological scope of 1 Corinthians 8:6 ("for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things") and anticipates the "new creation" language of 2 Corinthians 5:17 ("if anyone is in Christ, new creation"). The gospel is not merely a message about historical events; it is an act of new creation by the God who created all things.

The "outer person" and "inner person" of 4:16 anticipate 5:1-5, where the metaphors shift to tent and building, mortal and immortal, naked and clothed. The argument is continuous: the wasting outer person of 4:16 becomes the earthly tent of 5:1; the renewed inner person of 4:16 becomes the building from God of 5:1; the daily renewal of 4:16 connects to the Spirit as guarantee in 5:5.

The phrase "those who are perishing" (4:3) and the concept of destruction (apollymenoi/apollymi) connect back to 1 Corinthians 1:18 and forward to 2 Corinthians 2:15-16, where Paul described himself as the aroma of Christ "among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing" — "to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life." The division between those who perceive the gospel and those who are blinded runs throughout both letters.

The resurrection hope of 4:14 ("he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also") stands in direct continuity with the extended resurrection argument of 1 Corinthians 15. The God who raised Christ will raise those who belong to Christ. This is the same theological ground, applied here not as doctrine to be taught but as the living conviction that sustains an apostle under affliction.

The judgment-seat language that follows in 5:10 ("we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil") provides accountability to the entire chapter's argument. The apostle's transparency (4:2), his refusal to tamper with God's word, his faithful proclamation even under suffering — all of this will be evaluated. The renewal of the inner person is not automatic or inevitable; it is connected to faithfulness, to the deliberate gaze fixed on the unseen and eternal (4:18), and to the awareness that every person will give account. The perseverance Paul describes is not effortless confidence but a disciplined, costly, daily choice sustained by faith in the God who raises the dead.

div.title: 2 Corinthians 5 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author argues immediately before (2 Corinthians 4): Paul has been defending his apostolic ministry against the charge that his visible weakness disqualifies him. The chapter's thesis is stated at 4:7: "We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us." The treasure is the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6); the clay vessels are the apostle's fragile, afflicted, mortal body. Paul catalogued the paradoxes of apostolic life — afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not despairing, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed (4:8-9) — and grounded them in the death-and-life logic of the cross: the apostle carries the dying of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus is displayed in the same body (4:10-11). The chapter closed with a reframing of affliction as preparation for glory. "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (4:16). The "light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison" (4:17). Paul urged disciplined focus on what is unseen and eternal rather than what is seen and temporary (4:18), setting up the contrast between the temporal body and the eternal dwelling that opens chapter 5.

What the author argues immediately after (2 Corinthians 6:1-10): Paul continues without interruption from the appeal that closes chapter 5. "Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain" (6:1). The "working together" (synergountes) refers to the ambassadorial role described in 5:20 — Paul works together with God in making the appeal for reconciliation. He supports this appeal with a quotation from Isaiah 49:8 (LXX): "In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you" (6:2). Paul then declares: "Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (6:2b). The Isaiah passage is part of the Servant of the LORD oracle, and Paul applies it to the present moment — the time of reconciliation is now, and the Corinthians must not let it pass in vain. Paul then provides the most comprehensive catalogue of apostolic hardships in his letters (6:3-10), listing the afflictions, labors, and paradoxes that characterize his ministry: "in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger" (6:4-5), alongside the qualities that sustain him: "purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, truthful speech, the power of God" (6:6-7). The catalogue culminates in a series of paradoxes that echo 4:8-9: "as dying, and behold we live; as punished, and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything" (6:9-10). The entire section from 5:11 through 6:10 forms a continuous argument: the fear of the Lord drives the apostle (5:11), the love of Christ constrains him (5:14), the ministry of reconciliation defines his task (5:18-20), and the hardship catalogue demonstrates its cost and authenticity (6:3-10).

How chapter 5 connects the two: Chapter 5 occupies the final position in the three-chapter theological argument (3-5) about apostolic ministry, its glory, its apparent weakness, and its eschatological horizon. Chapter 3 established the surpassing glory of the new covenant. Chapter 4 explained why the minister of that glorious covenant appears so broken: the treasure is in clay vessels by design, so that the power is unmistakably God's. Chapter 5 completes the argument by answering two questions that chapter 4 leaves hanging. First: if the outer person is wasting away (4:16) and the visible is temporary (4:18), what happens when the wasting is complete — when the mortal body is destroyed? Paul answers in 5:1-5: the earthly tent is replaced by an eternal building from God, and the Spirit already given as a guarantee (1:22) assures this outcome. Second: given this eschatological hope, what governs the apostle's conduct in the present? Paul answers in 5:6-10: walking by faith, aiming to please the Lord, because everyone will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. These two answers — the certain hope and the present accountability — then generate the rest of the chapter. The certainty of judgment produces the "fear of the Lord" that drives Paul's persuasive ministry (5:11). The love of Christ, demonstrated in his death for all, constrains Paul to a life no longer self-directed (5:14-15). This produces a new mode of perception that evaluates nothing "according to the flesh" (5:16) and recognizes that those in Christ are a "new creation" (5:17). Finally, the theological ground of all this is stated: God has reconciled the world to himself through Christ, has entrusted the message of reconciliation to Paul, and Paul functions as God's ambassador, making God's own appeal through him (5:18-21). The chapter thus moves from eschatological hope through present accountability to the theological foundation of apostolic ministry, and 6:1 draws the immediate practical conclusion: do not receive this grace in vain.

div.title: Verses 1-5: The Earthly Tent and the Building from God
div.p: "For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (5:1).

The opening gar ("for") connects directly to 4:16-18. Paul has argued that the outer person wastes away while the inner person is renewed, that present affliction is temporary while future glory is eternal, and that the seen is transient while the unseen is permanent. The word "for" signals that 5:1 provides the ground for these assertions: the reason Paul can call affliction "light" and "momentary" is that he knows the mortal body is not his final dwelling.

The word "tent" (skenos) is rare — it appears only here and in verse 4 in the entire Greek scriptures and the LXX. However, the related word skene ("tent, tabernacle") pervades Israel's story. The skene was the tabernacle — the portable tent of God's presence during the wilderness period. Exodus 25:9 (LXX): "You shall make it according to all that I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle (skenes)." Exodus 40:34-35: "Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting (skenen tou martyriou), and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (skenen)." The tabernacle was by design temporary. It was the dwelling of God's presence during the transitional period between Egypt and the promised land, before the permanent temple was built. A first-century Jewish reader hearing "tent" in the context of a dwelling to be replaced by a permanent structure would immediately think of this trajectory: the temporary tabernacle yielding to the permanent temple.

Paul's metaphor follows the same trajectory. The "earthly tent" (he epigeios hemon oikia tou skenous — literally "our earthly house of the tent") is the mortal body, the "outer person" that is wasting away (4:16). The adjective epigeios ("earthly, on the earth, belonging to the earth") contrasts with the heavenly building that replaces it. The verb katalyo ("to destroy, to tear down, to dismantle") describes what happens to a tent: it is taken down, dismantled, its parts folded and removed. Paul does not use a word for violent destruction but for the methodical dismantling of a temporary structure. Death, in this metaphor, is not catastrophe but deconstruction of what was always temporary.

What replaces the tent is described with four phrases, each adding a layer of permanence. First: "a building from God" (oikodomen ek theou) — the word oikodome ("building, structure, edifice") describes a solid, permanent construction, in contrast to the collapsible tent. The source is "from God" (ek theou) — this is not something the person constructs but something received from God. Second: "a house not made with hands" (oikian acheiropoieton). The word acheiropoietos ("not made with hands, not of human manufacture") appears in Mark 14:58, where Jesus was accused of saying he would destroy "this temple made with hands" (cheiropoieton) and build another "not made with hands" (acheiropoieton). In Acts 7:48, Stephen declares, "the Most High does not dwell in houses made with hands (cheiropoietois)," quoting Isaiah 66:1. The word distinguishes divine craftsmanship from human manufacture. The resurrection body is God's work, not a product of human effort or natural process. Third: "eternal" (aionion) — the same word used in 4:17 for the "eternal weight of glory" and in 4:18 for the unseen things that are "eternal." The building does not deteriorate, does not need dismantling, does not belong to the temporary order. Fourth: "in the heavens" (en tois ouranois) — the location of the permanent dwelling is not the earthly sphere but the heavenly one. The contrast between epigeios ("earthly") and en tois ouranois ("in the heavens") is total.

The certainty is expressed by "we know" (oidamen) — not "we hope" or "we believe" but "we know." This is settled conviction, not speculation. The first person plural "we" continues the usage from 3:18 and 4:14-16, where "we" expanded from Paul and his apostolic team to include all who belong to the new covenant community. The knowledge Paul claims here is not private apostolic revelation but the shared conviction of the community that has the Spirit as guarantee (1:22, 5:5).
"For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling" (5:2).

The verb stenazo ("to groan, to sigh deeply") describes a sound of distress and longing produced by the pressure of present circumstances. The same verb appears in Romans 8:23: "we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies." The groaning in both passages is not despair but eager anticipation — the sound of those who know that their present condition is not final and who strain toward what is coming. The LXX uses stenazo for Israel's groaning in Egyptian bondage: Exodus 2:23, "the people of Israel groaned (katestenaxan) because of their slavery and cried out." Israel's groan in Egypt was the sound of an oppressed people awaiting deliverance that had been promised. Paul's groaning in the mortal body is the sound of one who awaits the deliverance that God has guaranteed.

The participle "longing" (epipothountes — "earnestly desiring, yearning for") describes the emotional posture behind the groaning. The verb epipotheo appears in 1:11 (Philippians), where Paul "longs" for the community with the affection of Christ, and in 7:7, 11 of this letter, where the Corinthians' "longing" (epipothesis) for Paul was part of the good news Titus brought. The longing is not vague; it is directed: "to put on our heavenly dwelling" (to oiketerion hemon to ex ouranou ependysasthai). The verb ependyomai ("to put on over, to be clothed upon, to put on as an outer garment over what is already worn") is critical. The prefix ep- ("upon, over") indicates putting something on over the top of what one already wears. Paul does not speak of exchanging one garment for another but of putting the heavenly dwelling on over the existing self. The imagery is of clothing, not replacement: the mortal is not discarded but covered over, enveloped, absorbed into something greater.
"If indeed, having put it on, we will not be found naked" (5:3).

The phrase is textually debated — some manuscripts read "having put on" (endysamenoi), others "having taken off" (ekdysamenoi). The reading endysamenoi ("having put on, having been clothed") fits the context better: Paul expresses confidence that when the heavenly dwelling is put on, he will not be found gymnos ("naked, bare, unclothed"). Nakedness in the LXX carries connotations of shame and exposure. Genesis 3:7: "Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked (gymnoi)." Genesis 3:10: "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked (gymnos), and I hid myself." Nakedness is the condition of exposure, vulnerability, and shame that results from the loss of what should cover a person. Paul's concern is not simply physical nudity but the state of being without a body — a disembodied existence stripped of the dwelling that belongs to the person. He does not want to be found in this condition.

This concern may reflect interaction with first-century views about the intermediate state between death and resurrection. Some Jewish traditions imagined the dead as disembodied souls awaiting the resurrection of the body. Paul's language suggests discomfort with this intermediate state: he wants to be clothed upon, not stripped bare. The preference is not for death (which would leave him temporarily unclothed) but for the transformation that puts on the heavenly dwelling without the intermediate state of nakedness.
"For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened — not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life" (5:4).

The verse restates and clarifies verse 2. The groaning is specified: it comes from being "burdened" (baroumenoi, "weighed down, oppressed"). The verb bareo appeared in 1:8 for the Asian affliction: "we were so utterly burdened (ebarethemen) beyond our strength." The weight is the pressure of mortality — not merely physical suffering but the entire condition of living in a body subject to decay, affliction, and death. This is the same burden described in 4:8-9 (afflicted, perplexed, persecuted, struck down) and in the "outer person wasting away" of 4:16.

Paul clarifies his desire with a negative and a positive. Negatively: "not that we would be unclothed" (ou thelomen ekdysasthai). He does not want mere escape from the body — the stripping away that death accomplishes. Positively: "but that we would be further clothed" (alla ependysasthai). The same verb from verse 2: to be clothed over, to have the heavenly dwelling put on over the mortal body. The purpose: "so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life" (hina katapothei to thneton hypo tes zoes). The verb katapino ("to swallow up, to consume, to engulf") appeared in 2:7, where the offender might be "swallowed up" by excessive sorrow. Here the swallowing is positive: mortality is consumed, absorbed, overwhelmed by life (zoe). The image is not destruction but transformation — what is mortal does not cease to exist but is taken up into life, as a drop of water is taken up by the sea.

The phrase echoes 1 Corinthians 15:54, where Paul quoted Isaiah 25:8: "Death is swallowed up (katepothei ho thanatos) in victory." In the Isaiah passage (LXX rendering differs from the Hebrew, but the concept persists), God's eschatological banquet on the mountain includes the swallowing up of death: "He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" (Isaiah 25:8, Hebrew). Paul applies the same verb and the same reversal: instead of death swallowing the living (which is death's present activity), life swallows mortality. The reversal is total: the predator becomes the prey.
"He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee" (5:5).

The subject is emphatic: God (ho theos) is the one who has prepared (ho katergasamenos) Paul and the community for this transformation. The verb katergazomai ("to prepare, to produce, to work out, to accomplish") is the same verb used in 4:17, where the light momentary affliction "is preparing" (katergazetai) an eternal weight of glory. The connection is deliberate: the affliction prepares the glory, and God has prepared the person for that glory. The two preparations are part of one divine work.

"For this very thing" (eis auto touto) — the demonstrative points to the transformation just described: the swallowing up of mortality by life, the clothing with the heavenly dwelling. This is not an accident or an afterthought; it is what God has been working toward in the believer from the beginning.

The guarantee is the Spirit: "who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee" (ho dous hemin ton arrabona tou pneumatos). This phrase is nearly identical to 1:22: "who has also sealed us and given us the Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee." The word arrabon ("guarantee, down payment, earnest money, first installment") was explained in its first appearance: a Semitic commercial term for the initial payment that legally binds the buyer to complete the transaction. The Spirit, already present in the community, is the first installment of the full eschatological inheritance. The Spirit's presence is not merely a promise of future transformation; it is the beginning of that transformation already underway. The inner renewal of 4:16, the transformation from glory to glory in 3:18, the writing on hearts of flesh in 3:3 — all of these are the Spirit's present work, and all of them function as the arrabon, the down payment, guaranteeing the full payment: the clothing with the heavenly dwelling, the swallowing up of mortality by life.

div.title: Verses 6-10: Confidence, Faith, and the Judgment Seat
div.p: "So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord" (5:6).

The inferential oun ("so, therefore") draws a conclusion from the preceding argument. Because God has prepared believers for the transformation and given the Spirit as guarantee, the apostle is "always of good courage" (pantote tharrountes). The verb tharreo ("to be of good courage, to be confident, to be bold") appeared in 7:16 ("I have complete confidence in you") and 10:1-2, where Paul hopes he will not have to use his boldness when present. Here it describes a settled disposition: despite the groaning, the burden, the wasting of the outer person, the apostle maintains confidence.

The sentence then states a spatial relationship between the present body and the Lord's presence. "At home in the body" (endemountes en to somati) uses the verb endemeo ("to be at home, to dwell in one's own country, to be among one's own people"). "Away from the Lord" (ekdemounen apo tou kyriou) uses the verb ekdemeo ("to be away from home, to be abroad, to be absent from one's own country"). The two verbs describe being a resident (endemos) or an expatriate (ekdemos). While the believer is at home in the mortal body, the believer is in a condition of being away from the Lord's immediate presence. This is not a statement about the Lord's absence from the believer's life — Paul has spent the entire letter describing the Spirit's presence (1:22, 3:3, 3:6, 3:8, 3:17-18, 5:5) and the glory that believers behold with unveiled faces (3:18). Rather, it describes a spatial and experiential gap: the full, face-to-face presence of the Lord awaits the transformation described in verses 1-5. The believer lives in the Lord's Spirit but has not yet arrived in the Lord's full presence.
"For we walk by faith, not by sight" (5:7).

The verse grounds the assertion of verse 6 with a gar ("for"). Walking "by faith" (dia pisteos) means navigating the present by trust in what has been promised but not yet seen. Walking "by sight" (dia eidous) means navigating by what is visible and tangible. The word eidos ("appearance, form, sight, visible shape") describes what can be directly perceived. The contrast between faith and sight recapitulates 4:18, where Paul looked at what is unseen rather than what is seen. The unseen realities — the building from God, the heavenly dwelling, the life that swallows mortality — are apprehended by faith, not by sight. The visible realities — the wasting body, the afflictions, the tent being dismantled — are real but temporary, and they do not determine the apostle's direction. Faith, not appearance, governs the walk.

The word peripateo ("to walk") is Paul's standard metaphor for the conduct of life. In 1 Corinthians 3:3, some in Corinth were "walking according to human standards" (kata anthropon peripateite). In 2 Corinthians 4:2, Paul described his ministry as not "walking in cunning" (me peripatountes en panourgia). Here, walking "by faith" is the mode of life that sustains the apostle between the present groaning and the future glory.
"Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (5:8).

Paul repeats the tharreo ("we are of good courage") from verse 6, reinforcing the confidence. The preference is stated clearly: given the choice, Paul "would rather" (eudokoumen mallon) be "away from the body" (ekdemesai ek tou somatos) and "at home with the Lord" (endemesai pros ton kyrion). The same endemos/ekdemos vocabulary from verse 6 is now reversed: instead of being at home in the body and away from the Lord, Paul prefers to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

This preference does not contradict the desire expressed in verses 2-4 for being "further clothed" rather than "unclothed." Paul's ideal is the transformation that puts on the heavenly dwelling without the intermediate state of nakedness (vv. 2-4). But given only two options — remaining in the mortal body, or departing and being with the Lord — Paul prefers the latter. The preference reveals that Paul's desire to remain in the body is not for its own sake but for the sake of his ministry. In Philippians 1:21-24, Paul expresses the same tension: "to live is Christ, and to die is gain... I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account." The dynamic is identical in both letters: Paul would rather be with the Lord, but his apostolic commission keeps him in the mortal body for the community's benefit.
"So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him" (5:9).

The word philotimeomai ("to make it one's ambition, to aspire earnestly, to strive eagerly") appears only three times in Paul's letters: here, in Romans 15:20 ("I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named"), and in 1 Thessalonians 4:11 ("aspire to live quietly"). The word carries the sense of earnest, honor-driven striving — the ambition of one who wants to be well-pleasing (euarestoi) to the Lord. The verb euaresteo ("to please, to be well-pleasing, to be acceptable") echoes LXX descriptions of those who pleased God. Genesis 5:24 (LXX): "Enoch was well-pleasing (euarestesen) to God, and was not found, because God took him." Hebrews 11:5 will later comment on this same tradition. The word describes a life oriented toward divine approval. Whether Paul is alive in the body or has departed to be with the Lord, his governing aim is unchanged: to please God. The present condition — embodied or disembodied, at home or away — does not alter the fundamental orientation of his life.
"For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil" (5:10).
The gar ("for") provides the ground for the striving of verse 9. The reason Paul makes it his aim to please the Lord is that all persons will give account.

"We must all appear" (tous pantas hemas phanerotheinai dei) — the verb dei ("it is necessary, it must") expresses divine necessity. The verb phaneroo ("to make manifest, to reveal, to lay bare") in the passive (phanerotheinai, "to be made manifest") means not merely to show up but to be fully exposed, laid open, displayed for what one truly is. The same verb has appeared throughout the letter for making things visible (2:14, 4:10-11, 5:11). At the judgment seat, there will be no concealment; the full reality of each person's life will be made manifest.

"The judgment seat of Christ" (to bema tou Christou) — the word bema refers to a raised platform from which a magistrate or governor rendered official judgments. In Corinth, the bema was a prominent architectural feature in the agora — the stone platform from which the Roman proconsul Gallio had presided when Paul himself was brought before him (Acts 18:12-17). The Corinthians knew what a bema looked like: they passed it in their daily commerce. Paul says that this bema belongs to Christ. The judge who will sit on the platform is not a Roman magistrate but the risen Messiah. The image transposes the familiar civic reality of Roman justice into the eschatological sphere: Christ will render judgment on the same pattern of public, authoritative, binding decision that the Corinthians associated with their own city's governance.

"So that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil" (hina komisetai hekastos ta dia tou somatos pros ha epraxen, eite agathon eite phaulon). The verb komizo ("to receive, to get back, to be requited") describes receiving something that is owed or earned — the recompense for one's actions. The evaluation is individual: "each one" (hekastos). The scope of the evaluation is "what he has done in the body" (ta dia tou somatos) — the deeds performed during embodied life. The standard is twofold: "whether good or evil" (eite agathon eite phaulon). The word agathon ("good") and phaulon ("worthless, bad, evil, morally deficient") describe the quality of the deeds. The word phaulon is not the stronger word for evil (kakon or poneron) but a word that emphasizes triviality, worthlessness, the failure to live up to what was possible. The judgment evaluates not only overt wickedness but the failure to pursue good.

The statement includes everyone: tous pantas hemas, "all of us." Paul does not exempt himself or any category of believer from this judgment. The apostle who carries the treasure of the gospel in a clay vessel, who has been anointed, sealed, and given the Spirit as guarantee — this same apostle will stand before the judgment seat and give account. The Spirit's presence as arrabon does not render the judgment unnecessary; it is the down payment on a transaction that will be completed at the judgment. The believer's life between the arrabon and the completion is the life that will be evaluated.

The verse echoes LXX descriptions of divine judgment. Psalm 62:12 (LXX 61:13): "For you will render to each one according to his work (kata ta erga autou)." Proverbs 24:12: "Does he not who weighs the heart perceive it?... Will he not repay each according to his work (kata ta erga autou)?" Ecclesiastes 12:14: "For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil." The principle that God judges according to deeds is fundamental to Israel's scriptures. Paul applies it to the bema of Christ, identifying Christ as the one who exercises the divine prerogative of judgment.

div.title: Verses 11-13: The Fear of the Lord, Transparency, and the Apostle's Posture
div.p: "Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience" (5:11).

The oun ("therefore") draws a consequence from the judgment-seat statement. "The fear of the Lord" (ton phobon tou kyriou) is one of the most established phrases in the LXX. Proverbs 1:7: "The fear of the LORD (phobos kyriou) is the beginning of knowledge." Proverbs 9:10: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Psalm 19:9 (LXX 18:10): "The fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever." Psalm 111:10 (LXX 110:10): "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding." Isaiah 11:2: "the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD (phobon kyriou)." The "fear of the Lord" is not terror but the reverential awareness of standing before a holy, just, and all-seeing God — the awareness that one's life is transparent to the divine gaze. Paul "knows" (eidotes, "having known, being aware of") this fear because he has just stated its ground: everyone will appear before Christ's judgment seat.

This fear drives Paul's activity: "we persuade others" (anthropous peithomen). The verb peitho ("to persuade, to convince, to win over") describes the apostolic task of bringing people to the point of accepting the gospel message. Paul is not passive; he actively persuades, and the motivation is the awareness that people face judgment. The persuasion is not manipulation (Paul has renounced cunning and tampering with God's word, 4:2) but the urgent effort to present the truth so that people will receive it.

"But what we are is known to God" (theo de pephanerometha) — the verb phaneroo appears again in the perfect passive: "we have been made manifest to God." Paul's inner reality — his motives, his sincerity, his character — is fully visible to God. There is no concealment, no gap between appearance and reality, in God's perception of Paul. The appeal to God's knowledge of Paul's heart echoes 1:12, where Paul's boast was "the testimony of our conscience" — his inner awareness before God.

"And I hope it is known also to your conscience" (elpizo de kai en tais syneidesesin hymon pephanerousthai). Paul shifts from certainty (God knows) to hope (the Corinthians may also know). The word syneidesis ("conscience, inner moral awareness") appeared in 1:12 and 4:2 in connection with Paul's transparency. Paul hopes that the Corinthians' own conscience, their internal faculty of moral evaluation, recognizes what God already knows: that Paul is genuine, not a peddler or a manipulator. The hope implies that some in Corinth have not yet reached this recognition. The rival teachers and their influence have clouded the Corinthians' perception of Paul, and Paul is working to restore clarity.

"We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart" (5:12).

The self-commendation question that surfaced in 3:1 ("Are we beginning to commend ourselves again?") returns. The verb synistanein ("to commend, to recommend") appeared in 3:1, 4:2, and will appear again in 6:4, 10:12, 10:18, and 12:11 — it is one of the letter's running concerns. Paul denies that his argument constitutes self-commendation. Instead, he says he is providing the Corinthians with material for their defense of him: "giving you cause to boast about us" (aphermen didontes hymin kauchematos hyper hemon). The word aphorme ("opportunity, occasion, starting point, base of operations") is a military term for a base from which to launch an operation. Paul is giving the Corinthians a base from which to defend his ministry.

The defense is needed against specific opponents: "those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart" (tous en prosopo kauchomenous kai me en kardia). The word prosopon ("face, outward appearance, surface") is the same word that has tracked through chapters 2-4 in connection with Moses' face, Christ's face, and unveiled faces. Here it describes the mode of evaluation used by Paul's rivals: they boast in what is visible, in external credentials, in impressive appearances. The contrast is with kardia ("heart") — the inner reality that is hidden from surface inspection but visible to God (5:11). The rival teachers evaluate and commend themselves by appearances; Paul's commendation rests on the inner reality that God sees and that Paul hopes the Corinthians' conscience also recognizes.
"For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you" (5:13).

The verb existemi ("to be beside oneself, to be out of one's mind, to be ecstatic, to be amazed") describes a state in which a person appears to have lost normal mental control. In Mark 3:21, Jesus' family came to seize him because people said "he is out of his mind" (exeste). In Acts 26:24, Festus told Paul, "You are out of your mind (maine); your great learning is driving you out of your mind (eis manian)." The charge of madness or ecstasy could refer to several aspects of Paul's behavior: his willingness to endure suffering that seemed insane by worldly standards, his ecstatic spiritual experiences (Paul will mention being "caught up to the third heaven" in 12:2-4), or his seemingly irrational conduct as judged by the standards of the sophists and rhetoricians the Corinthians admired.

Paul does not deny the charge; he redirects it. If he is "beside himself" (exestemen), it is "for God" (theo) — directed toward God, in God's service, for God's purposes. If he is "in his right mind" (sophronoumen), it is "for you" (hymin) — directed toward the community's benefit. The verb sophroneo ("to be of sound mind, to be sober, to be reasonable, to exercise self-control") describes the state of measured, rational, controlled thinking. Whether Paul appears mad or sane, the orientation is never self-serving: it is either Godward or community-directed. The verse anticipates the paradox catalogue of 6:8-10 ("as deceivers, and yet true... as having nothing, yet possessing everything"), where Paul's apostolic life defies conventional categories of evaluation.

div.title: Verses 14-15: The Love of Christ and the Death That Reorients All Living
div.p: "For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died" (5:14).

The gar ("for") provides the deeper motivation behind the apostle's conduct — deeper than the fear of judgment (v. 11), deeper than the defense against critics (v. 12), deeper than the question of sanity (v. 13). The driving force of Paul's entire ministry is stated: "the love of Christ controls us" (he agape tou Christou synechei hemas).

The verb synecho ("to hold together, to compress, to constrain, to control, to press from every side") is powerful. In Luke 8:45, the crowd "pressed in" (syneichon) on Jesus. In Luke 12:50, Jesus said, "I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress (synechomai) until it is accomplished!" In Luke 19:43, enemies will "hem you in (synexousin) on every side." In Philippians 1:23, Paul was "hard pressed (synechomai) between the two" — living and dying. The verb describes being gripped, held in, compressed by a force that leaves no room for other motivations. The love of Christ is not one factor among many in Paul's decision-making; it is the constraining pressure that shapes everything.

The genitive "of Christ" (tou Christou) is most naturally read as subjective: Christ's love for Paul and for all people. This is confirmed by what follows: the content of the love is Christ's dying for all. The love in view is not Paul's love for Christ but Christ's demonstrated love in dying. The same direction is found in Romans 5:8: "God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." The love is demonstrated in the act of dying.

The conclusion Paul has reached (krinantes, "having judged, having concluded, having determined") provides the content of this constraining love: "one has died for all, therefore all have died" (heis hyper panton apethanen, ara hoi pantes apethanon). The logic is compact. The "one" (heis) is Christ. He died "for all" (hyper panton) — the preposition hyper ("on behalf of, for the sake of") indicates that Christ's death was substitutionary and representative: he died in the place of all and on behalf of all. The conclusion drawn from this representative death is that "all have died" (hoi pantes apethanon). If the one who died represented all, then in his death, all died. The death of all is not a separate event from Christ's death; it is contained within it. When the representative dies, those he represents die with him.

The word pantes ("all") is universal in scope. Paul does not say "all believers" or "all the elect" but "all" — all human beings for whom Christ died. The scope of the death matches the scope of the representation. However, the consequence of this universal death is worked out in verse 15, where "those who live" are distinguished from the universal "all" by their response.
"And he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (5:15).

The purpose (hina, "so that, in order that") of Christ's death is now stated. He died for all "so that those who live" (hoi zontes, "the living ones") — those who, having died with Christ in his representative death, now live in the new reality that his resurrection opens — "might no longer live for themselves" (meketi heautois zosin). The negation meketi ("no longer") implies a previous state: before Christ's death, all people lived for themselves. The death of Christ ended that self-directed existence and inaugurated a new one.

The new direction of life: "for him who for their sake died and was raised" (alla to hyper auton apothanonti kai egerthenti). The One who died and was raised becomes the orienting center of the living person's existence. Life is no longer organized around the self but around Christ. The passive participle egerthenti ("having been raised") identifies God as the agent of Jesus' resurrection — the same pattern as 4:14 ("he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also") and 1:9 ("the God who raises the dead").

The phrase "those who live" (hoi zontes) functions as a distinguishing marker within the universal "all" of verse 14. Christ died for all, and therefore all died. But the purpose of that death — living for Christ rather than for self — is actualized only by "those who live." The language implies a condition: the reorientation from self to Christ is the defining characteristic of those who participate in the life that Christ's death and resurrection made possible. This is not automatic; it is described as the purpose for which Christ died, and its actualization depends on the living person's response.

div.title: Verses 16-17: Knowing According to the Flesh and the New Creation
div.p: "From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer" (5:16).

The phrase "from now on" (apo tou nyn) marks a temporal boundary. Since the conclusion of verses 14-15 — that Christ's death for all has ended self-directed existence and inaugurated a new orientation — a new mode of perception has replaced the old. The inferential hoste ("therefore, so that, consequently") draws the consequence.

"We regard no one according to the flesh" (oudena oidamen kata sarka) — the verb oida ("to know, to regard, to recognize, to perceive") describes how Paul evaluates people. The phrase kata sarka ("according to the flesh") defines the mode of evaluation, not its object. Paul does not say "we don't know anyone's body" but "we don't evaluate anyone by the standards of the flesh." The fleshly standard of evaluation is the standard used by those who "boast about outward appearance" (5:12) — the standard that measures people by their rhetoric, their credentials, their letters of recommendation, their visible power and impressiveness. Paul's rivals in Corinth have been operating kata sarka, and the Corinthians have been susceptible to this evaluation. Paul declares that this mode of assessment is over.

"Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh" (ei kai egnokamen kata sarka Christon) — the concessive clause acknowledges that Paul himself once operated by this standard. The perfect tense egnokamen ("we have known, we have regarded") describes a past state of knowing that Paul has now abandoned. "Regarding Christ according to the flesh" most naturally refers to evaluating the Messiah by fleshly criteria: visible power, political authority, worldly impressiveness. Before Paul's encounter with the risen Christ on the Damascus road, he evaluated Jesus kata sarka — as a crucified criminal, a failed pretender, someone whose shameful death disqualified him from being the Messiah. A Messiah who was crucified violated every expectation built on fleshly evaluation. The Damascus road shattered that evaluation.

"We regard him thus no longer" (alla nyn ouketi ginoskomen) — the shift is complete. The Christ Paul now knows is not evaluated by the standards of visible power and worldly success but by the standards revealed in the cross: power in weakness, life through death, glory in shame. This is the same reversal that drove 1 Corinthians 1:18-25, where the word of the cross was foolishness to those operating by human wisdom and the power of God to those being saved.

The verse also applies to how Paul evaluates people in general, including himself and the Corinthians. If no one is evaluated kata sarka, then the criteria the rival teachers have used to measure Paul — his weak bodily presence, his unimpressive speech (10:10), his lack of external credentials — are irrelevant. The criteria by which Paul evaluates himself and commends his ministry are not fleshly but spiritual: the Spirit's transforming work, the community's existence as a letter of Christ, the treasure carried in clay vessels.
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (5:17).

The inferential hoste ("therefore") draws the conclusion from the preceding argument. The phrase "if anyone is in Christ" (ei tis en Christo) establishes the condition. The prepositional phrase en Christo ("in Christ") has been Paul's consistent marker for the sphere of divine action throughout both letters: God "leads us in Christ" (2:14), "establishes us in Christ" (1:21), the promises are affirmed "in Christ" (1:20), the veil is removed "in Christ" (3:14). To be "in Christ" is to be located within the reality defined by Christ's death and resurrection.

The declaration is stark: kaine ktisis ("new creation"). There is no verb in the Greek — the phrase is a bare predicate: "new creation." The verbal austerity reinforces the force of the statement: the reality is so fundamental it needs no grammatical elaboration. The person in Christ is a new creation.
